title: An Introductory Course to Judgment Aggregation
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1607.03307v1
published: 2016-07-12T10:57:30Z
summary: Reaching some form of consensus is often necessary for autonomous agents that want to coordinate their actions or otherwise engage in joint activities. One way to reach a consensus is by aggregating individual information, such as decisions, beliefs, preferences and constraints. Judgment aggregation is a social choice method, which generalises voting, that studies the aggregation of individual judgments regarding the truth-value of logically related propositions. As such, judgment aggregation is applicable for consensus reaching problems in multi agent systems. As other social choice theory, judgment aggregation research is abundant with impossibility results. However, the aim of this tutorial is to give an introduction to the methods of judgment aggregation, not the impossibility results. In particular, the tutorial will introduce the basic frameworks that model judgment aggregation problems and give an overview of the judgment aggregation functions so far developed as well as their social theoretic and computational complexity properties. The focus of the tutorial are consensus reaching problems in multi agent systems that can be modelled as judgment aggregation problems. The desirable properties of a judgment aggregation method applied to these problems are not necessarily the same as properties desirable in legal or political contexts, which is considered to be the native domain of judgment aggregation. After this tutorial the participants are expected to be able to read and understand judgment aggregation literature and have a grasp on the state-of-the-art and open questions in judgment aggregation research of interest to multi agent systems.

title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18126v1
published: 2026-10-13T10:37:12Z
summary: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.
